title: Reading the code symbols
intro: The code in this book is set in a font that joins some characters into a single shape. `=>` prints as an arrow and `===` as one long bar. Nothing changes at the keyboard: you still type the separate characters in the middle column. This key lists every combination that joins somewhere in the book.

rows.meaning: Strict equality.
Strict inequality.
Loose inequality. The book uses it only as `!= null`, which rules out both `null` and `undefined`.
Less than or equal to, greater than or equal to.
Logical AND: the right side runs only when the left is truthy.
Logical OR: the right side runs only when the left is falsy.
Nullish coalescing: the right side is used only when the left is `null` or `undefined`.
Optional chaining: the access stops, giving `undefined`, when the left is `null` or `undefined`.
Separates an arrow function's parameters from its body, or a function type's parameters from its return type.
An optional property or parameter. `?` makes it optional, and `:` starts its type.
Spread or rest. In comments and strings, it just means text left out.
Add one, subtract one. In commands, `--` starts a long option such as `--noEmit`.
Starts a comment that runs to the end of the line.
Start and end a block comment.
Starts a documentation comment.
Two or three type-argument lists closing together.
Closing brackets next to each other.
Two underscores in a name.
The parent folder in a file path.
The old-file and new-file headers in a diff.
